summary: This RFC adds an authentication trailer to OSPFv3, so packets can be authenticated without relying on IPsec, which was the only option before and can be hard to configure and maintain. It brings OSPFv3 closer to the approach used by other routing protocols. It was replaced by RFC 7166.

plainLanguage.summary: Routers used to need a complicated lock to prove messages were real. This adds a simpler stamp on each message instead. Later, a newer RFC replaced it.

subtitle: Authenticating OSPFv3 routing messages without depending on IPsec.

tldr.problem: OSPFv3 (OSPF for IPv6) originally relied on IPsec for authentication, but IPsec is complex to configure and maintain, especially in environments like mobile ad hoc networks where it is impractical.
tldr.mechanism: This document adds an authentication trailer to the end of OSPFv3 packets, using HMAC with SHA algorithms to sign routing messages in a way similar to how OSPFv2 works.
tldr.outcome: OSPFv3 deployments can now authenticate packets without depending on IPsec, making the protocol more practical in challenging environments. RFC 6506 was replaced by RFC 7166.

today: RFC 6506 is now Historic, replaced by RFC 7166, which provides updated guidance on OSPFv3 authentication trailer usage.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
OSPFv3 is the version of OSPF (Open Shortest Path First) designed for IPv6. Unlike OSPFv2 (which runs on IPv4), OSPFv3 does not include authentication fields in its packet headers. Instead, it depends entirely on IPsec to provide authentication and integrity protection through the Authentication Header (AH) and Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) extension headers.

However, in some environments, particularly Mobile Ad Hoc Networks (MANETs) where routers are frequently mobile and connectivity is dynamic, IPsec is difficult to configure and maintain. The IPsec approach also lacks replay protection when using manual key configuration (which is typical for routing protocol authentication), and it makes it hard to prioritize certain packet types like Hello packets.

This document defines an alternative: an authentication trailer appended to the end of OSPFv3 packets that provides authentication using HMAC (Hashed Message Authentication Code) and cryptographic hash algorithms, similar to how OSPFv2 authenticates packets.
sections.plainLanguage: IPv6 routers needed complex encryption to authenticate each other. This RFC lets them use a simpler method: a stamp at the end of each message that proves it came from someone with the right key.

sections.title: How Authentication Trailer Works
sections.content:
Instead of relying on IPsec, routers using this mechanism append a data block called an authentication trailer to the end of each OSPFv3 packet. The trailer is included in the IPv6 payload length but not in the OSPFv3 packet's own length field, following the same pattern as OSPFv2.

A new AT-bit (Authentication Trailer bit) in the OSPFv3 Options field indicates whether authentication trailers are in use. Routers MUST set this bit in Hello and Database Description packets to signal that all packets on the link will include an authentication trailer. Other packet types inherit the setting from the neighbor data structure.

The trailer contains four main elements: an authentication type field (currently only HMAC Cryptographic Authentication is defined), the length of the authentication data, a Security Association ID (SAID) that identifies which key and algorithm to use, a 64-bit sequence number for replay protection, and the variable-length authentication data (message digest).
sections.plainLanguage: At the end of each routing message, add a signature block. The block says which key to use, a counter to prevent replay attacks, and a cryptographic checksum of the message.

sections.title: Security Associations and Keys
sections.content:
An OSPFv3 Security Association (SA) is a set of parameters shared between two legitimate OSPF routers. Each SA has an identifier (a 16-bit number configured by the network operator), an authentication algorithm, and an authentication key.

The supported algorithms are HMAC-SHA-1, HMAC-SHA-256, HMAC-SHA-384, and HMAC-SHA-512. Implementations MUST support HMAC-SHA-256 as the default algorithm and SHOULD support HMAC-SHA-1. The key length varies depending on the algorithm.

Each SA also specifies key lifetime parameters: when to start accepting packets with that key, when to start using it for generating packets, when to stop generating packets with it, and when to stop accepting packets with it. This allows smooth key transitions: the new key's accept time can start before its generation time, and the old key's generation can stop before its acceptance stops, ensuring no gap in authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: Before routers can authenticate each other, they must be configured with the same key and agree on which algorithm to use. The key has a lifetime, so routers can switch to a new key without breaking the conversation.

sections.title: Authenticating Packets
sections.content:
The authentication process starts by obtaining the current time and the system's EUI-64 identifier (or deriving one from the MAC address or serial number). These are combined with the authentication key, and the result is hashed using SHA-256 to create a cryptographic key (Ko). A cryptographic sequence number—a strictly increasing 64-bit counter—is included in the trailer and incremented for every packet transmitted.

To compute the message digest, the router first fills the authentication data field with a padding value (Apad). It then computes an inner hash: the cryptographic key XORed with an inner padding pattern, concatenated with the entire OSPFv3 packet and any optional Link-Local Signaling data block. Next, it computes an outer hash: the cryptographic key XORed with an outer padding pattern, concatenated with the inner hash result. This outer hash becomes the authentication data transmitted in the trailer.

When receiving a packet, the router extracts the sequence number and compares it to the last accepted sequence number from that neighbor: if the new number is not greater, the packet is a replay and is discarded. The router then verifies the message digest using the same procedure. If verification fails, the packet is dropped. On successful verification, the sequence number is recorded for future replay checks.

The IPv6 source address is included in the authentication computation to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks where an attacker modifies the source address in a Hello packet.
sections.plainLanguage: To sign a message, compute a hash of the message plus the key, then hash that result again. To verify, do the same computation and check if the signatures match. Also keep track of packet numbers to spot replays.

sections.title: Security and Migration
sections.content:
This authentication method does not provide confidentiality—the routing information remains visible in plain text. It does, however, authenticate that the packet came from a router with access to the correct key, preventing unauthorized routers from injecting false routing information.

It is not assumed that the CNAME authentication proves the specific originating router, only that the packet came from someone with the correct key. Deployments SHOULD use sufficiently long and random authentication keys (at least 128 pseudo-random bits) to prevent guessing and cryptographic attacks. Management systems SHOULD support hexadecimal input of keys for better entropy.

The mechanism does not prevent impersonation by participants who have the key (they can already send valid signatures); it prevents unauthorized parties without the key from forging messages. Secure RTP (SRTP) can provide additional security if needed.

To migrate existing networks, all OSPFv3 routers on a link SHOULD be updated simultaneously. If a gradual migration is necessary, a transition mode allows routers to include authentication in sent packets while not verifying it in received packets, easing the cutover. After migration is complete, routers should be configured to drop unauthenticated packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone with the key can forge signatures (they already have the key), so this protects against outsiders, not insiders. Use strong keys, and switch all routers at once if you can. If you must migrate gradually, run in a mode where new routers sign packets but accept both signed and unsigned packets temporarily.

fields.name: Authentication Type
fields.desc: Type of authentication; 1 for HMAC Cryptographic Authentication.

fields.name: Auth Data Length
fields.desc: Total length of the trailer including fixed header and variable digest.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Reserved field; set to 0 when sending, ignored when receiving.

fields.name: Security Association ID
fields.desc: Identifies the algorithm and secret key used to create the digest.

fields.name: Sequence Number (High 32 bits)
fields.desc: High-order 32 bits of a 64-bit strictly increasing counter.

fields.name: Sequence Number (Low 32 bits)
fields.desc: Low-order 32 bits of a 64-bit strictly increasing counter.
